questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The seed-section figure shows an embryo enclosed by a seed coat and a fruit wall derived from the ovary. Which inference is best supported?
options: A) The plant must be a gymnosperm
B) The ovule was enclosed in an ovary before fruit development
C) The seed contains no embryo
D) The fruit wall formed from the pollen grain
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) The ovule was enclosed in an ovary before fruit development.
Why: A fruit wall (pericarp) develops from the wall of the ovary. If the seed lies inside a fruit wall, the ovule from which it formed must have been inside an ovary. Ovules enclosed in an ovary are the defining feature of angiosperms.
Why not the others: (A) Gymnosperms have naked ovules and seeds; they form no ovary and no fruit. (C) The figure shows an embryo inside the seed coat. (D) A pollen grain is the male gametophyte; it delivers the male gametes and does not form any part of the fruit.
Key point: Ovary → fruit; ovule → seed; ovary wall → pericarp.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.topic: Structural Organisation In Plants And Animals
questions.question: Use the root cross-section in the figure. Which identification and vascular arrangement fit?
options: A) Monocot root with many radial xylem poles
B) Dicot stem with scattered bundles
C) Dicot root with radial xylem and phloem
D) Monocot stem with closed collateral bundles
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Dicot root with radial xylem and phloem.
Why: The figure shows a central star of xylem with four arms, and patches of phloem lying between the arms, so xylem and phloem are on different radii. This radial arrangement is found in roots. Two to four xylem groups with little or no pith is the dicot pattern.
Why not the others: (A) A monocot root has many xylem groups (usually more than six) around a large pith. (B) A dicot stem has conjoint bundles arranged in a ring, not a central xylem star. (D) A monocot stem has many scattered conjoint closed bundles.
Key point: Root: radial bundles. Dicot root: 2–4 xylem groups. Monocot root: many groups and a large pith.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Two glucose residues join by a covalent bond after removal of one H₂O molecule. Which linkage type is formed in a disaccharide?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Glycosidic bond.
Why: Two monosaccharides join when the –OH group on the anomeric carbon of one reacts with an –OH group of the other, and a molecule of water is removed. The C–O–C link formed is a glycosidic bond. Maltose, for example, has two glucose units joined by an α-1,4 glycosidic bond.
Why not the others: (A) A peptide bond (–CO–NH–) joins amino acids. (B) A phosphodiester bond joins nucleotides through a phosphate group. (C) An ester bond joins a fatty acid to glycerol in fats.
Key point: Sugars: glycosidic. Amino acids: peptide. Nucleotides: phosphodiester.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Unripe bananas are kept in three sealed bags. Bag 1 holds bananas only. Bag 2 also holds a ripe apple, and its bananas ripen much faster. Bag 3 holds a ripe apple together with a pad soaked in potassium permanganate, which oxidises unsaturated hydrocarbon gases; its bananas ripen no faster than those in bag 1. Which inference do the three results support?
options: A) The ripe apple gives off ethylene, a gaseous hormone that speeds ripening, and the pad removes it
B) The ripe apple supplies sugars that pass through the air into the bananas
C) Potassium permanganate releases oxygen, which stops respiration in the bananas
D) The ripe apple gives off abscisic acid, which the pad converts to gibberellin
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) The ripe apple gives off ethylene, a gaseous hormone that speeds ripening, and the pad removes it.
Why: The effect passes through the air inside a sealed bag, so the signal must be a gas. Ripening fruits give off ethylene (CH₂=CH₂), which raises the rate of respiration and brings on ripening in other fruits. Potassium permanganate oxidises the double bond of ethylene; with the gas removed, the apple has no effect. Bag 1 is the control that shows the normal rate.
Why not the others: (B) Sugars are not volatile and cannot travel through air from one fruit to another. (C) The pad absorbs a gas; it does not stop respiration, and the bananas in bag 3 ripen at the normal rate of bag 1. (D) Abscisic acid is not a gas and is a growth inhibitor; hormones are not converted into one another in this way.
Key point: Ethylene is the only gaseous plant hormone; it promotes ripening.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: At an active tissue, CO₂ rises and pH falls while the incoming arterial blood is unchanged. What effect on haemoglobin helps deliver more O₂ locally?
options: A) A left shift and stronger O₂ binding
B) A right shift and lower O₂ affinity
C) No change because blood pH cannot vary
D) Conversion of O₂ into CO₂ inside haemoglobin
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) A right shift and lower O₂ affinity.
Why: In active tissue the partial pressure of CO₂ is high, the H⁺ concentration is high (low pH) and the temperature is raised. All three shift the oxygen dissociation curve to the right. At the same partial pressure of O₂, haemoglobin then holds less oxygen, so more is released to the tissue.
Why not the others: (A) A left shift means tighter binding, which would hold oxygen back; that happens in the lungs. (C) Blood pH does vary slightly between arteries and active tissue. (D) Haemoglobin carries oxygen; it does not turn it into carbon dioxide.
Key point: High CO₂, high H⁺, high temperature: curve shifts right, O₂ is unloaded.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Some plants, such as Viola and Oxalis, bear cleistogamous flowers in addition to ordinary ones. Why do cleistogamous flowers set seed even when no pollinators are present?
options: A) They are pollinated by wind
B) They produce seeds without forming gametes
C) They never open, so pollen from the anthers falls on the stigma of the same flower
D) Their pollen grains are carried by water
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) They never open, so pollen from the anthers falls on the stigma of the same flower.
Why: In a cleistogamous flower the anthers and stigma lie close together inside the closed bud. When the anthers split, the pollen lands on the stigma of the same flower. No outside agent is needed, and no foreign pollen can enter, so seed set is assured.
Why not the others: (A) Wind cannot carry pollen into or out of a closed flower. (B) Seed formation without gametes is apomixis, a different process. (D) Pollination by water occurs in a few aquatic plants such as Vallisneria.
Key point: Cleistogamy: closed flowers, always self-pollinated, seed set assured.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Two equally large isolated populations each follow Hardy–Weinberg proportions: their A-allele frequencies are 0.8 and 0.2. They are pooled for sampling before any cross-population mating. How does the pooled heterozygote fraction compare with the Hardy–Weinberg expectation calculated from pooled p=0.5?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Observed 0.32; expected 0.50.
Given: Population 1: p = 0.8, q = 0.2. Population 2: p = 0.2, q = 0.8. Equal sizes; each in Hardy–Weinberg proportions.
Formula/Principle: Heterozygote frequency in one population = 2pq.
Step 1: Population 1: 2 × 0.8 × 0.2 = 0.32. Population 2: 2 × 0.2 × 0.8 = 0.32.
Step 2: Pooled sample, observed heterozygotes = (0.32 + 0.32)/2 = 0.32.
Step 3: Pooled allele frequency p = (0.8 + 0.2)/2 = 0.5, so expected heterozygotes = 2 × 0.5 × 0.5 = 0.50.
Why: The Hardy–Weinberg rule assumes random mating within one population. A mixture of two groups that have not interbred is not one random-mating population, so it shows fewer heterozygotes than the rule predicts from the pooled allele frequency.
Why not the others: (A) 0.50 would be seen only after one generation of random mating between the two groups. (B) 0.68 is the pooled frequency of homozygotes, not heterozygotes. (C) reverses the roles and uses 0.25, the expected frequency of one homozygote.
Key point: A deficit of heterozygotes can mean the sample mixes separate populations.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: In the fermentation figure, identify microbes P and Q from their observed products. Which pair is consistent?
options: A) P is yeast; Q is Lactobacillus
B) P is Lactobacillus; Q is yeast
D) P is a virus; Q is a cyanobacterium
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) P is yeast; Q is Lactobacillus.
Why: Yeast (Saccharomyces) ferments sugar to ethanol and carbon dioxide; the gas makes dough rise. Lactic acid bacteria such as Lactobacillus ferment sugar to lactic acid, which curdles milk, and give off no gas. The products shown for P are those of yeast and the product shown for Q is that of Lactobacillus.
Why not the others: (B) has the two microbes the wrong way round. (C) Methanogens produce methane from cellulose-rich material in the absence of oxygen; methane is not among the products shown. (D) A virus has no metabolism and ferments nothing, and a cyanobacterium is a photosynthetic organism.
Key point: Yeast: ethanol + CO₂. Lactobacillus: lactic acid.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The figure shows a vector opened with two different restriction enzymes, E and H, and an insert prepared with matching E and H ends. Their sticky overhang sequences are noncompatible with one another. Why is insertion favoured in one orientation?
options: A) Both ends are identical, so either orientation works
B) Each insert end can anneal only to its corresponding vector end, then ligase seals the aligned backbone
C) The E end can ligate to both E and H sites equally
D) The insert has no phosphates, so orientation is irrelevant
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Each insert end can anneal only to its corresponding vector end, then ligase seals the aligned backbone.
Why: Each restriction enzyme leaves its own single-stranded overhang. An E overhang pairs only with another E overhang, and an H overhang only with an H overhang. The insert therefore fits the opened vector one way round. DNA ligase then joins the sugar–phosphate backbones.
Why not the others: (A) The two ends are different, which is the whole point of using two enzymes. (C) The stem says the E and H overhangs are not compatible, so an E end cannot pair with an H end. (D) Ligase needs the 5′ phosphate groups to seal the nicks, and phosphates do not decide the orientation.
Key point: Two different enzymes give directional cloning.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: A population grows by 20% annually at low density, but in later years additions diminish as size nears a stable level while births continue. Which description fits the later regime?
options: A) Constant exponential growth with unlimited resources
C) Density-limited approach to carrying capacity
D) A fixed annual decrease regardless of density
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Density-limited approach to carrying capacity.
Why: At low density, resources are plentiful and the population grows at a constant percentage, which is exponential growth. As numbers rise, each individual gets a smaller share of the resources, so the yearly addition falls and the size levels off at the carrying capacity K. This is logistic growth, dN/dt = rN(K − N)/K.
Why not the others: (A) Exponential growth would keep adding 20% each year without limit. (B) The population settles at a stable level; it does not die out. (D) Numbers still rise slowly; they do not fall by a fixed amount.
Key point: Logistic growth: growth slows as N approaches K.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The forelimbs of a whale, a bat, a cheetah and a human do different jobs but are built from the same set of bones: humerus, radius, ulna, carpals, metacarpals and phalanges. What are such organs called, and what do they indicate?
options: B) Vestigial organs; use and disuse
D) Homologous organs; divergent evolution from a common ancestor
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Homologous organs; divergent evolution from a common ancestor.
Why: Organs with the same basic structure and origin but different functions are homologous. The same bones have been modified for swimming, flying, running and grasping. This shows that these mammals share a common ancestor and that the limb changed in different directions to meet different needs, which is divergent evolution.
Why not the others: (A) Analogous organs have different structures but the same function, such as the wings of a butterfly and a bird; they arise by convergent evolution. (B) Vestigial organs are reduced and functionless; these limbs are fully used. (C) Analogous organs do not indicate common ancestry.
Key point: Homologous: same structure, different function. Analogous: different structure, same function.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: In snapdragon (Antirrhinum), a true-breeding red-flowered plant crossed with a true-breeding white-flowered plant gives an F₁ that is entirely pink. When the F₁ plants are self-pollinated, what phenotypic ratio is expected in the F₂?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 1 red : 2 pink : 1 white.
Why: Neither allele is completely dominant, so the heterozygote Rr is pink, in between RR (red) and rr (white). Selfing Rr gives the genotypes 1 RR : 2 Rr : 1 rr. Because each genotype has its own phenotype, the phenotypic ratio is the same as the genotypic ratio.
Why not the others: (B) 3 : 1 is the F₂ ratio when one allele is completely dominant. (C) 1 : 1 is a test-cross ratio and leaves out the pink class. (D) 9 : 3 : 4 belongs to a two-gene cross with epistasis.
Key point: Incomplete dominance: F₂ phenotypic ratio = genotypic ratio = 1 : 2 : 1.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Fraction of the glomerular filtrate reabsorbed
questions.question: In a healthy adult the glomerular filtration rate is about 125 mL per minute, and about 1.5 L of urine is passed per day. About what percentage of the filtrate is reabsorbed by the renal tubules?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) About 99%.
Given: GFR = 125 mL per minute; urine = 1.5 L per day.
Formula/Principle: Volume reabsorbed = volume filtered − volume of urine.
Step 1: Filtrate per day = 125 mL × 60 × 24 = 180 000 mL = 180 L.
Step 2: Reabsorbed = 180 − 1.5 = 178.5 L.
Step 3: Percentage = 178.5 ÷ 180 × 100 = 99.2%, about 99%.
Why: The kidneys filter a very large volume of plasma each day, and nearly all of it is taken back by the tubules, most of it in the proximal convoluted tubule. Only about one part in a hundred leaves as urine.
Why not the others: (A) 90% reabsorbed would leave 18 L of urine a day. (C) 50% would leave 90 L. (D) About 1% is the fraction excreted, not the fraction reabsorbed.
Key point: 180 L filtered per day, about 1.5 L excreted.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Metal ion as an enzyme cofactor
questions.question: A purified protein-digesting enzyme loses its activity when a chelating agent removes its zinc ions, although the protein itself is undamaged. Activity returns when zinc ions are added back. What is the role of zinc in this enzyme?
options: A) It is the substrate of the enzyme
B) It is a competitive inhibitor
C) It is a cofactor, without which the protein part (apoenzyme) is inactive
D) It supplies the amino acids of the active site
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) It is a cofactor, without which the protein part (apoenzyme) is inactive.
Why: Many enzymes need a non-protein part, called a cofactor, to work. The protein part alone is the apoenzyme. Metal ions are one kind of cofactor; they form coordinate bonds with side chains at the active site and with the substrate. Zinc is the cofactor of the protein-digesting enzyme carboxypeptidase. Removing it stops the activity and adding it back restores it, while the protein stays intact.
Why not the others: (A) The substrate is the protein being digested, and it is used up; zinc is not. (B) An inhibitor lowers activity when it is added; here activity falls when zinc is taken away. (D) Amino acids of the active site are part of the protein chain, which is undamaged.
Key point: Apoenzyme + cofactor = active enzyme (holoenzyme).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.topic: Structural Organisation In Plants And Animals
questions.sub_topic: Sieve tube elements and companion cells
questions.question: A mature sieve tube element of an angiosperm has cytoplasm but no nucleus. Which cell controls its functions?
options: A) A tracheid lying next to it
D) The companion cell joined to it by pit fields
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) The companion cell joined to it by pit fields.
Why: A sieve tube element loses its nucleus as it matures, although it keeps a layer of cytoplasm and a large vacuole. Each element lies beside a companion cell, a specialised parenchyma cell with a nucleus. The two are connected through pit fields in their common wall, and the nucleus of the companion cell controls the activities of the sieve tube.
Why not the others: (A) Tracheids are dead cells of the xylem and carry water. (B) Phloem fibres are dead sclerenchyma cells that give strength. (C) Xylem parenchyma stores food and helps the sideways movement of water in the xylem; it is not linked to sieve tubes.
Key point: Sieve tube element: living, no nucleus. Companion cell: supplies the control.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Which of the following chlorides has the greatest covalent character?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) LiCl.
Why: No ionic bond is purely ionic. A small cation with a high charge density pulls the electron cloud of the anion towards itself (polarisation), which gives the bond some covalent character. All four cations have a charge of +1, so the smallest one, Li⁺, polarises the chloride ion most. This is why LiCl dissolves in organic solvents such as ethanol.
Why not the others: (B) Na⁺ is larger than Li⁺ and polarises less. (C) K⁺ is larger still. (D) Cs⁺ is the largest ion of the group, so CsCl is the most ionic of the four.
Key point: Smaller cation, larger anion, higher charge: more covalent character.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: The figure shows ionisation isomers X and Y. Their aqueous samples receive BaCl₂ separately. Which sample yields immediate BaSO₄ from a free counter-ion?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Only X.
Why: Ions written outside the square bracket are free in solution; ligands inside the bracket are bonded to the metal and are not free. X is [Co(NH₃)₅Br]SO₄, which gives free SO₄²⁻ ions; these react at once with Ba²⁺ to give white BaSO₄. Y is [Co(NH₃)₅SO₄]Br, in which sulfate is a ligand, so no precipitate forms with BaCl₂.
Why not the others: (A) Y has bromide, not sulfate, as its free ion; it would give a precipitate with AgNO₃ instead. (C) Only one of the two has free sulfate. (D) X does have free sulfate.
Key point: Ionisation isomers give different ions in solution.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Why do the actinoids show a wider range of oxidation states than the lanthanoids?
options: A) Actinoids have no f electrons
C) The 5f, 6d and 7s levels are of comparable energy
D) Actinoid nuclei are stable and never decay
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) The 5f, 6d and 7s levels are of comparable energy.
Why: In the actinoids the 5f, 6d and 7s orbitals lie close together in energy, so electrons from all three can take part in bonding. The early actinoids therefore reach high oxidation states: +4 for Th, +5 for Pa, +6 for U and +7 for Np. In the lanthanoids the 4f electrons are buried more deeply, and +3 is by far the most common state.
Why not the others: (A) Actinoids are the elements in which the 5f subshell is being filled. (B) All actinoids are metals. (D) All actinoids are radioactive; this does not explain their oxidation states.
Key point: Lanthanoids: mainly +3. Actinoids: +3 to +7.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.question: Lithium differs from the other alkali metals in several ways, for example in forming a nitride and in the low solubility of its carbonate and fluoride. Which element of group 2 does it resemble most closely?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Magnesium.
Why: Lithium resembles magnesium, the element diagonally below it to the right. Li⁺ and Mg²⁺ have similar sizes and similar charge-to-radius ratios, so their compounds behave alike: both metals form a nitride (Li₃N, Mg₃N₂), both carbonates decompose easily on heating, and both have sparingly soluble carbonates and fluorides.
Why not the others: (A) Beryllium is next to lithium in the period; its diagonal partner is aluminium. (B) Calcium is much larger, and its properties are closer to those of sodium. (C) Barium is larger still and far more reactive.
Key point: Diagonal pairs: Li–Mg, Be–Al, B–Si.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Energy of one mole of photons
questions.question: What is the energy of one mole of photons of wavelength 400 nm? (h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, N_A = 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) About 299 kJ mol⁻¹.
Given: \(\lambda=400\ \mathrm{nm}=4.00\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm m\); \(h=6.626\times10^{-34}\ \mathrm{J\,s}\); \(c=3.0\times10^{8}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\); \(N_A=6.022\times10^{23}\ \mathrm{mol^{-1}}\).
Formula/Principle: Energy of one photon \(E=\dfrac{hc}{\lambda}\); energy of one mole \(=N_AE\).
Step 1: \(E=\dfrac{6.626\times10^{-34}\times3.0\times10^{8}}{4.00\times10^{-7}}=4.97\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm J\).
Step 2: Multiply by the Avogadro constant.
Worked derivation: \[N_AE=6.022\times10^{23}\times4.97\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm J=2.99\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}\approx299\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}\]
Why: Light is absorbed and emitted in packets called photons, each of energy hc/λ. A mole of photons is called an einstein. The value is of the same order as covalent bond enthalpies, which is why violet and ultraviolet light can break bonds.
Why not the others: (B) 120 kJ mol⁻¹ is the value for 1000 nm. (C) 598 kJ mol⁻¹ is the value for 200 nm; energy is inversely proportional to wavelength. (D) 4.97 × 10⁻¹⁹ is the energy of one photon in joules, not of a mole in kilojoules.
Key point: \(E_{\text{mol}}=\dfrac{N_Ahc}{\lambda}\).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: A 250 mL sample of 0.40 M acid HA is diluted to 500 mL. A 100 mL aliquot of the diluted acid reacts 1:1 with NaOH. How many moles of NaOH are needed for complete neutralisation?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 0.020 mol.
Given: 250 mL of 0.40 M HA diluted to 500 mL; 100 mL aliquot; HA : NaOH = 1 : 1.
Formula/Principle: On dilution \(M_1V_1=M_2V_2\); \(n=MV\).
Step 1: \(M_2=\dfrac{0.40\times250}{500}=0.20\ \mathrm M\).
Step 2: Moles of HA in the aliquot \(=0.20\ \mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}}\times0.100\ \mathrm L\).
Worked derivation: \[n(\ce{HA})=0.20\times0.100=0.020\ \mathrm{mol};\qquad n(\ce{NaOH})=n(\ce{HA})=0.020\ \mathrm{mol}\]
Why: Dilution lowers the concentration but does not change the amount of acid: the whole 500 mL still holds 0.10 mol. The aliquot is one fifth of the diluted solution, so it holds one fifth of the acid.
Why not the others: (A) 0.010 mol halves the concentration twice. (C) 0.040 mol uses the original concentration, 0.40 M, for the aliquot. (D) 0.100 mol is the acid in the whole 500 mL, not in the aliquot.
Key point: Dilute first (M₁V₁ = M₂V₂), then take the aliquot (n = MV).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: Follow the electron-flow arrows in the carbonyl addition figure. Which role does CN⁻ play in the bond-forming step?
options: A) Electrophile accepting an electron pair
B) Leaving group departing from a saturated carbon
C) Nucleophile donating a pair to an electrophilic carbon
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Nucleophile donating a pair to an electrophilic carbon.
Why: The carbonyl carbon carries a partial positive charge because oxygen is more electronegative. The curved arrow starts at the lone pair on the carbon of CN⁻ and ends at this carbon, so cyanide gives an electron pair to form the new C–C bond. A species that donates an electron pair to carbon is a nucleophile. The π electrons move to oxygen, which is later protonated to give a cyanohydrin.
Why not the others: (A) An electrophile accepts an electron pair; here that is the carbonyl carbon. (B) Cyanide is being added, not lost, and the carbon attacked is sp², not a saturated carbon. (D) Cyanide has no hydrogen to donate; it is the conjugate base of HCN.
Key point: The tail of a curved arrow is the electron source: the nucleophile.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: A ring has CH₃ at carbon 1 and Br at carbon 4. Under mild nitration, both groups direct ortho/para but they favour different available positions. Which site is favoured mainly by the more activating group, assuming steric effects do not reverse the directing effect?
options: A) Carbon 4 already occupied by Br
B) Carbon 3 or 5, meta to CH₃
C) Carbon 1 already occupied by CH₃
D) Carbon 2 or 6, ortho to CH₃
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Carbon 2 or 6, ortho to CH₃.
Why: The methyl group activates the ring by its +I effect and hyperconjugation and directs to its ortho and para positions. Bromine also directs ortho and para through its lone pairs, but it deactivates the ring by its −I effect. When two groups compete, the more strongly activating one decides. The position para to methyl is taken by bromine, so the nitro group enters ortho to methyl, at carbon 2 or 6.
Why not the others: (A) Carbon 4 already carries bromine; substitution replaces hydrogen. (B) Carbons 3 and 5 are ortho to bromine and meta to methyl; they are favoured by the weaker, deactivating director. (C) Carbon 1 already carries the methyl group.
Key point: The stronger activator controls the position of substitution.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: 2-Bromobutane is heated with alcoholic KOH. What is the major organic product?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) But-2-ene.
Why: Alcoholic KOH removes HBr from a haloalkane (β-elimination) to give an alkene. In 2-bromobutane a hydrogen can be lost from C-1 or from C-3. Saytzeff's rule says the major product is the alkene with more alkyl groups on the double-bonded carbons, because it is more stable. Loss of hydrogen from C-3 gives but-2-ene, CH₃CH=CHCH₃, which has two alkyl groups on the double bond.
Why not the others: (B) But-1-ene, formed by loss of hydrogen from C-1, has only one alkyl group on the double bond and is the minor product. (C) Butan-2-ol is the substitution product obtained with aqueous KOH. (D) Butane would need reduction, not elimination.
Key point: Alcoholic KOH: elimination. Aqueous KOH: substitution. The more substituted alkene predominates.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Phenol is treated with chloroform and aqueous NaOH, and the mixture is then acidified. What is the main organic product?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 2-Hydroxybenzaldehyde (salicylaldehyde).
Why: This is the Reimer–Tiemann reaction. Chloroform and NaOH give dichlorocarbene, an electrophile. It attacks the electron-rich phenoxide ring, mainly at the ortho position, to give a –CHCl₂ group. Alkali hydrolyses this to –CHO, and acidification frees the phenolic –OH.
Why not the others: (A) Benzoic acid has no –OH on the ring; the phenolic group is not removed. (C) Chlorobenzene would need the –OH to be replaced by Cl, which does not happen. (D) Salicylic acid is formed in the Kolbe reaction, where sodium phenoxide reacts with CO₂, or when CCl₄ is used in place of CHCl₃.
Key point: Phenol + CHCl₃/NaOH → o-hydroxybenzaldehyde. Phenoxide + CO₂ → o-hydroxybenzoic acid.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: When an egg is boiled, the clear egg white becomes an opaque solid. Which levels of protein structure are destroyed in this change, and which is kept?
options: A) The primary structure is destroyed; the secondary and tertiary structures are kept
B) All three levels are destroyed, giving free amino acids
C) The secondary and tertiary structures are destroyed; the primary structure is kept
D) No level changes; water simply evaporates
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) The secondary and tertiary structures are destroyed; the primary structure is kept.
Why: Heat breaks the hydrogen bonds and other weak interactions that hold a protein in its folded shape. The helices uncoil and the globular molecule unfolds; the unfolded chains tangle and set solid. The peptide bonds are not broken, so the sequence of amino acids is unchanged.
Why not the others: (A) is the reverse of what happens; the amino acid sequence survives while the folding is lost. (B) Breaking the chain into amino acids is hydrolysis, which needs acid, alkali or enzymes. (D) The change is a chemical change in the protein, not drying.
Key point: Denaturation destroys 2° and 3° structure and biological activity; 1° structure remains.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: What is the pH of a 0.0050 M solution of Ba(OH)₂ at 298 K, assuming complete dissociation?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 12.0.
Given: \([\ce{Ba(OH)2}]=0.0050\ \mathrm M\); complete dissociation; 298 K, \(\mathrm pK_w=14\).
Formula/Principle: \(\ce{Ba(OH)2 -> Ba^2+ + 2OH-}\); \(\mathrm{pOH}=-\log[\ce{OH-}]\); \(\mathrm{pH}=14-\mathrm{pOH}\).
Step 1: \([\ce{OH-}]=2\times0.0050=0.010\ \mathrm M\).
Step 2: \(\mathrm{pOH}=-\log(1.0\times10^{-2})=2.0\).
Worked derivation: \[\mathrm{pH}=14.0-2.0=12.0\]
Why: Each formula unit of barium hydroxide gives two hydroxide ions, so the hydroxide concentration is twice the concentration of the base. The solution is alkaline, so the pH must be above 7.
Why not the others: (A) 2.0 is the pOH, not the pH. (B) 11.7 takes \([\ce{OH-}]=0.0050\ \mathrm M\), forgetting the factor of two. (C) 12.3 doubles twice, taking \([\ce{OH-}]=0.020\ \mathrm M\).
Key point: For M(OH)₂: [OH⁻] = 2 × concentration; pH + pOH = 14 at 298 K.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: From the freezing-point graph for a 0.10 m electrolyte A₂B solution and the displayed solvent constant, estimate its degree of dissociation into three ions.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) About 0.63.
Given: From the figure: \(\Delta T_f=0.00-(-0.42)=0.42\ \mathrm K\); \(K_f=1.86\ \mathrm{K\,kg\,mol^{-1}}\); \(m=0.10\ \mathrm{mol\,kg^{-1}}\); \(\ce{A2B -> 2A+ + B^2-}\) (3 ions).
Formula/Principle: \(\Delta T_f=iK_fm\); for a solute giving n ions, \(i=1+(n-1)\alpha\).
Step 1: \(i=\dfrac{\Delta T_f}{K_fm}=\dfrac{0.42}{1.86\times0.10}=2.26\).
Step 2: \(i=1+2\alpha\).
Worked derivation: \[\alpha=\frac{i-1}{2}=\frac{2.26-1}{2}=0.63\]
Why: Freezing-point depression counts particles. With no dissociation the depression would be 0.186 K, and with complete dissociation into three ions it would be 0.558 K. The measured 0.42 K lies between the two, so the salt is partly dissociated.
Why not the others: (B) 0.26 is close to \(i-2\), which has no meaning here. (C) 0.42 is the depression itself, read off as if it were α. (D) 1.26 is \(i-1\) without dividing by 2; a degree of dissociation cannot exceed 1.
Key point: \(\alpha=\dfrac{i-1}{n-1}\).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: A 0.20 M solution of KCl has a conductivity of 0.0248 S cm⁻¹ at 298 K. What is its molar conductivity?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 124 S cm² mol⁻¹.
Given: \(\kappa=0.0248\ \mathrm{S\,cm^{-1}}\); \(c=0.20\ \mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}}\).
Formula/Principle: \(\Lambda_m=\dfrac{\kappa\times1000}{c}\), with κ in S cm⁻¹ and c in mol L⁻¹.
Step 1: 1 L = 1000 cm³, so \(c=0.20\ \mathrm{mol}/1000\ \mathrm{cm^3}=2.0\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{mol\,cm^{-3}}\).
Worked derivation: \[\Lambda_m=\frac{0.0248\ \mathrm{S\,cm^{-1}}\times1000\ \mathrm{cm^3\,L^{-1}}}{0.20\ \mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}}}=124\ \mathrm{S\,cm^2\,mol^{-1}}\]
Why: Conductivity is the conductance of a unit cube of solution. Molar conductivity is the conductance of all the ions from one mole of electrolyte, so the conductivity is divided by the concentration. The factor 1000 changes litres to cubic centimetres.
Why not the others: (A) 4.96 multiplies by the concentration instead of dividing. (C) 0.124 leaves out the factor 1000. (D) 248 uses 0.10 M in place of 0.20 M.
Key point: \(\Lambda_m=\kappa/c\); watch the units.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Use ΔHf° (kJ mol⁻¹): CH₄(g)=−75, CO₂(g)=−394, H₂O(l)=−286, O₂(g)=0. What is ΔH° for CH₄+2O₂→CO₂+2H₂O(l)?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) −891.
Given: \(\Delta_fH^\circ\) in kJ mol⁻¹: \(\ce{CH4(g)}=-75\); \(\ce{CO2(g)}=-394\); \(\ce{H2O(l)}=-286\); \(\ce{O2(g)}=0\).
Formula/Principle: \(\Delta_rH^\circ=\sum\Delta_fH^\circ(\text{products})-\sum\Delta_fH^\circ(\text{reactants})\).
Step 1: Products: \(-394+2(-286)=-966\).
Step 2: Reactants: \(-75+2(0)=-75\).
Worked derivation: \[\Delta_rH^\circ=-966-(-75)=-891\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}\]
Why: By Hess's law the enthalpy change does not depend on the route. The reaction can be pictured as breaking methane into its elements (+75) and then forming the products from the elements (−966). Combustion is exothermic, so the answer must be negative.
Why not the others: (A) −680 = −394 − 286 counts only one mole of water and leaves out methane. (B) +891 has the wrong sign. (D) −755 = −394 − 286 − 75 counts one mole of water and adds the −75 of methane when it should be subtracted.
Key point: Products minus reactants, each multiplied by its coefficient.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: For the ellipse x²/16+y²/12=1, what are its eccentricity and the positive x-directrix coordinate?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 1/2 and 8.
Given: \(\dfrac{x^2}{16}+\dfrac{y^2}{12}=1\Rightarrow a^2=16,\ b^2=12\)
Formula/Principle: \(e=\sqrt{1-\dfrac{b^2}{a^2}},\quad\text{directrix}:\ x=\dfrac ae\)
Step 1: \(e=\sqrt{1-\dfrac{12}{16}}=\sqrt{\dfrac14}=\dfrac12\)
Worked derivation: \[x=\frac ae=\frac{4}{1/2}=8\]
Check: \[c=ae=2,\quad c^2=a^2-b^2=16-12=4\]
Why: \(b^2=a^2(1-e^2)\)
Why not the others: (A) \(e=\dfrac{c^2}{a^2}=\dfrac14,\ x=16\); (B) \(x=a=4\); (C) \(e=\dfrac ba=\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\).
Key point: \(\text{foci }(\pm ae,0),\ \text{directrices }x=\pm\dfrac ae\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Parametric horizontal tangent and second derivative
questions.question: A parametric curve has \(x=t^2+1,\ y=t^3-3t\), with \(t>0\). At its horizontal tangent, what are the tangent equation and the value of \(d^2y/dx^2\)?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(y=-2;\ 3/2\).
Given: \(x=t^2+1,\quad y=t^3-3t,\quad t>0\)
Formula/Principle: \(\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{dy/dt}{dx/dt},\quad\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=\dfrac{\frac{d}{dt}\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)}{dx/dt}\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{3t^2-3}{2t}=0\Rightarrow t=1\)
Step 2: \(t=1:\ x=2,\ y=-2\Rightarrow\text{tangent }y=-2\)
Step 3: \(\dfrac{d}{dt}\left(\dfrac{3t}{2}-\dfrac{3}{2t}\right)=\dfrac32+\dfrac{3}{2t^2}\)
Worked derivation: \[\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}=\frac{\frac32+\frac{3}{2t^2}}{2t}\Bigg|_{t=1}=\frac{3}{2}\]
Check: \[\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}>0\Rightarrow\text{local minimum of }y\text{ at }(2,-2)\]
Why: \(\text{horizontal tangent}\iff\dfrac{dy}{dt}=0,\ \dfrac{dx}{dt}\ne0\)
Why not the others: (B) \(x=2\) (vertical line); (C) \(\dfrac32+\dfrac32=3\) (not divided by \(\dfrac{dx}{dt}\)); (D) \(y(1)=-2\ne2\).
Key point: \(\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}\ne\dfrac{d^2y/dt^2}{d^2x/dt^2}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: What is the finite area enclosed by y=x² and y=2x−x²?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 1/3.
Given: \(y=x^2,\quad y=2x-x^2\)
Formula/Principle: \(A=\displaystyle\int_{x_1}^{x_2}\left(y_{\text{upper}}-y_{\text{lower}}\right)dx\)
Step 1: \(x^2=2x-x^2\Rightarrow2x(x-1)=0\Rightarrow x=0,\ 1\)
Step 2: \(0<x<1:\ 2x-x^2>x^2\)
Worked derivation: \[A=\int_0^1\left(2x-2x^2\right)dx=\left[x^2-\frac{2x^3}{3}\right]_0^1=1-\frac23=\frac13\]
Check: \[x=\tfrac12:\ \tfrac34-\tfrac14=\tfrac12>0\]
Why: \(\text{the curves meet only at }x=0\text{ and }x=1\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\displaystyle\int_0^1(x-x^2)\,dx=\frac16\); (C) \(\displaystyle\int_0^1(2x-x^2)\,dx=\frac23\); (D) \(\displaystyle\int_0^12x\,dx=1\).
Key point: \(\text{find the intersections first}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: Consider f: ℝ→[0,∞) defined by f(x)=x². Which classification is correct?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Surjective but not injective.
Given: \(f:\mathbb R\to[0,\infty),\quad f(x)=x^2\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{injective}:\ f(x_1)=f(x_2)\Rightarrow x_1=x_2;\quad\text{surjective}:\ \text{range}=\text{codomain}\)
Step 1: \(f(1)=f(-1)=1,\ 1\ne-1\Rightarrow\text{not injective}\)
Step 2: \(y\ge0:\ f(\sqrt y)=y\Rightarrow\text{range}=[0,\infty)\)
Worked derivation: \[\text{range}=[0,\infty)=\text{codomain}\Rightarrow\text{surjective}\]
Check: \[y=4:\ x=\pm2\ (\text{two pre-images})\]
Why: \(\text{the codomain is }[0,\infty),\ \text{not }\mathbb R\)
Why not the others: (A) \(f(1)=f(-1)\); (B) \(f(1)=f(-1)\); (D) \(\text{range}=[0,\infty)\).
Key point: \(\text{surjectivity depends on the stated codomain}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: For a 3×3 matrix A with det A=−2, what is tr(A adj A)?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) −6.
Given: \(A\in\mathbb R^{3\times3},\quad\det A=-2\)
Formula/Principle: \(A\,\operatorname{adj}A=(\det A)\,I\)
Step 1: \(A\,\operatorname{adj}A=-2I_3\)
Worked derivation: \[\operatorname{tr}(-2I_3)=3\times(-2)=-6\]
Check: \[A=\operatorname{diag}(1,1,-2):\ \operatorname{adj}A=\operatorname{diag}(-2,-2,1),\ A\operatorname{adj}A=\operatorname{diag}(-2,-2,-2)\]
Why: \(\operatorname{tr}(kI_n)=nk\)
Why not the others: (A) \(-2=\det A\); (B) \(2\times(-2)=-4\) (\(n=2\)); (C) \(+6\) (sign).
Key point: \(A\,\operatorname{adj}A=\operatorname{adj}A\,A=(\det A)I\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: Events A and B are independent with P(A)=1/2 and P(B)=1/3. What is P(A∪B)?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 2/3.
Given: \(P(A)=\tfrac12,\quad P(B)=\tfrac13,\quad A,B\ \text{independent}\)
Formula/Principle: \(P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B),\quad P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B)\)
Step 1: \(P(A\cap B)=\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac13=\tfrac16\)
Worked derivation: \[P(A\cup B)=\frac12+\frac13-\frac16=\frac23\]
Check: \[1-P(A')P(B')=1-\frac12\cdot\frac23=\frac23\]
Why: \(\text{independent}\ne\text{mutually exclusive}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\tfrac12+\tfrac13=\tfrac56\) (\(P(A\cap B)=0\) assumed); (C) \(\tfrac16=P(A\cap B)\); (D) \(\tfrac12=P(A)\).
Key point: \(P(A\cup B)=1-P(A')P(B')\ \text{for independent events}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: Five distinct people sit at a round table; rotations count as the same arrangement. How many arrangements have A and B not adjacent?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 12.
Given: \(5\ \text{distinct people, round table, rotations identical}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{circular arrangements of }n=(n-1)!\)
Step 1: \(\text{total}=4!=24\)
Step 2: \(A,B\ \text{adjacent}:\ (AB)\ \text{as one unit}\Rightarrow(4-1)!\times2=12\)
Worked derivation: \[24-12=12\]
Check: \[\text{fix }A;\ B\ \text{in 2 of 4 seats not next to }A;\ \text{others }3!:\ 2\times6=12\]
Why: \(\text{not adjacent}=\text{total}-\text{adjacent}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(3!=6\); (C) \(24-6=18\) (factor 2 omitted); (D) \(4!=24\) (total).
Key point: \(\text{fix one person to remove rotations}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Weighted binomial coefficient sums via finite differentiation
questions.question: Write \((1+x)^6=\sum_{k=0}^{6}c_kx^k\). What is \(\sum_{k=0}^{6}k^2c_k\)?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 672.
Given: \((1+x)^6=\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^6c_kx^k,\quad c_k=\binom6k\)
Formula/Principle: \(\left(x\dfrac{d}{dx}\right)^2\displaystyle\sum c_kx^k=\sum k^2c_kx^k\)
Step 1: \(x\dfrac{d}{dx}(1+x)^n=nx(1+x)^{n-1}\)
Step 2: \(x\dfrac{d}{dx}\left[nx(1+x)^{n-1}\right]=nx(1+x)^{n-1}+n(n-1)x^2(1+x)^{n-2}\)
Step 3: \(x=1:\ \displaystyle\sum k^2c_k=n2^{n-1}+n(n-1)2^{n-2}\)
Worked derivation: \[n=6:\ 6\times32+30\times16=192+480=672\]
Check: \[0+6+60+180+240+150+36=672\]
Why: \(k^2\binom nk\ \text{is generated by applying }x\dfrac{d}{dx}\ \text{twice}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(192=\displaystyle\sum kc_k\); (B) \(480=\displaystyle\sum k(k-1)c_k\); (D) \(1344=2\times672\).
Key point: \(\displaystyle\sum k^2\binom nk=n(n+1)2^{n-2}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: Let \(S_N=\sum_{n=1}^{N}1/[n(n+1)(n+2)]\). What is the least positive integer N for which S_N>1/5?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 2.
Given: \(S_N=\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^N\frac{1}{n(n+1)(n+2)}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\dfrac{1}{n(n+1)(n+2)}=\dfrac12\left[\dfrac{1}{n(n+1)}-\dfrac{1}{(n+1)(n+2)}\right]\)
Step 1: \(S_N=\dfrac12\left[\dfrac12-\dfrac{1}{(N+1)(N+2)}\right]\)
Step 2: \(S_1=\dfrac12\left[\dfrac12-\dfrac16\right]=\dfrac16<\dfrac15\)
Worked derivation: \[S_2=\frac12\left[\frac12-\frac1{12}\right]=\frac{5}{24}=0.208>\frac15\]
Check: \[S_2=\frac16+\frac1{24}=\frac{5}{24}\]
Why: \(S_N\ \text{increases with }N\ \text{and}\ S_N\to\dfrac14\)
Why not the others: (A) \(S_1=\dfrac16<\dfrac15\); (B) \(N=3>2\) (not least); (C) \(N=10>2\) (not least).
Key point: \(\text{telescoping sum: only the first and last terms survive}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: For real a, define \(L(a)=\lim_{x\to0}(|x-a|-|a|)/x\), if a finite two-sided limit exists. Which statement is complete?
options: A) It exists for all a≠0 and equals −sgn(a); at a=0 it fails
B) It exists for all a and equals 0
C) It exists only for a=0 and equals 1
D) It exists for all a>0 and nowhere else
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) It exists for all a≠0 and equals −sgn(a); at a=0 it fails.
Given: \(L(a)=\displaystyle\lim_{x\to0}\frac{|x-a|-|a|}{x}\)
Formula/Principle: \(L(a)=\dfrac{d}{dx}|x-a|\Big|_{x=0}\)
Step 1: \(a>0,\ |x|<a:\ |x-a|=a-x\Rightarrow\dfrac{a-x-a}{x}=-1\)
Step 2: \(a<0,\ |x|<|a|:\ |x-a|=x-a,\ |a|=-a\Rightarrow\dfrac{x-a+a}{x}=+1\)
Step 3: \(a=0:\ \dfrac{|x|}{x}=\begin{cases}+1,&x>0\\-1,&x<0\end{cases}\)
Worked derivation: \[L(a)=-\operatorname{sgn}(a)\ \ (a\ne0);\qquad L(0)\ \text{does not exist}\]
Check: \[a=2,\ x=0.1:\ \frac{1.9-2}{0.1}=-1;\qquad a=-2,\ x=0.1:\ \frac{2.1-2}{0.1}=+1\]
Why: \(|x-a|\ \text{is differentiable everywhere except at }x=a\)
Why not the others: (B) \(L(2)=-1\ne0\); (C) \(L(0)\ \text{does not exist}\); (D) \(L(-2)=+1\ \text{exists}\).
Key point: \(\dfrac{d}{dx}|x-a|=\operatorname{sgn}(x-a),\ x\ne a\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: A quantity y(t)>0 follows dy/dt=2ty and starts at y(0)=3. What is its value at t=1?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 3e.
Given: \(\dfrac{dy}{dt}=2ty,\quad y(0)=3,\quad y>0\)
Formula/Principle: \(\displaystyle\int\frac{dy}{y}=\int2t\,dt\)
Step 1: \(\ln y=t^2+C\)
Step 2: \(t=0:\ \ln3=C\)
Step 3: \(y=3e^{t^2}\)
Worked derivation: \[y(1)=3e^{1}=3e\approx8.15\]
Check: \[\frac{d}{dt}\left(3e^{t^2}\right)=2t\cdot3e^{t^2}=2ty\]
Why: \(\text{variables separable}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(e^2\); (C) \(3e^{2t}\big|_{t=1}=3e^2\) (\(\int2t\,dt=2t\)); (D) \(6e\).
Key point: \(\dfrac{dy}{dt}=g(t)\,y\Rightarrow y=y_0e^{\int_0^tg\,dt}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: The lines L₁: (x,y,z)=(t,0,0) and L₂: (x,y,z)=(0,1+s,1) extend indefinitely. What is their shortest distance?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 1.
Given: \(L_1:\ \mathbf r=t(1,0,0);\quad L_2:\ \mathbf r=(0,1,1)+s(0,1,0)\)
Formula/Principle: \(d=\dfrac{|(\mathbf a_2-\mathbf a_1)\cdot(\mathbf d_1\times\mathbf d_2)|}{|\mathbf d_1\times\mathbf d_2|}\)
Step 1: \(\mathbf d_1\times\mathbf d_2=(1,0,0)\times(0,1,0)=(0,0,1)\)
Step 2: \(\mathbf a_2-\mathbf a_1=(0,1,1)\)
Worked derivation: \[d=\frac{|(0,1,1)\cdot(0,0,1)|}{1}=1\]
Check: \[L_1\subset\{z=0\},\ L_2\subset\{z=1\}\Rightarrow d=1\]
Why: \(\text{the common perpendicular is along }\mathbf d_1\times\mathbf d_2\)
Why not the others: (A) \(z=0\ne z=1\Rightarrow\text{no intersection}\); (B) \(|(0,1,1)|=\sqrt2\) (distance between the two base points); (D) \(2\ne1\).
Key point: \(\text{project }\mathbf a_2-\mathbf a_1\ \text{on }\mathbf d_1\times\mathbf d_2\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: A line in space makes an angle of 60° with the positive x-axis and 45° with the positive y-axis. What acute angle does it make with the z-axis?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 60°.
Given: \(\alpha=60^\circ,\quad\beta=45^\circ\)
Formula/Principle: \(\cos^2\alpha+\cos^2\beta+\cos^2\gamma=1\)
Step 1: \(\cos^2\gamma=1-\dfrac14-\dfrac12=\dfrac14\)
Step 2: \(\cos\gamma=\pm\dfrac12\)
Worked derivation: \[\gamma=60^\circ\ \ (\text{acute})\]
Check: \[\left(\tfrac12\right)^2+\left(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\right)^2+\left(\tfrac12\right)^2=1\]
Why: \((l,m,n)\ \text{is a unit vector}\Rightarrow l^2+m^2+n^2=1\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\cos^230^\circ=\tfrac34\ne\tfrac14\); (B) \(\cos^245^\circ=\tfrac12\ne\tfrac14\); (C) \(\cos^290^\circ=0\ne\tfrac14\).
Key point: \(l^2+m^2+n^2=1\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Variance of the first n even natural numbers
questions.question: The variance of the first n even natural numbers 2, 4, 6, …, 2n is 8. What is n?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 5.
Given: \(x_k=2k,\ k=1,\dots,n;\quad\sigma^2=8\)
Formula/Principle: \(\operatorname{Var}(1,2,\dots,n)=\dfrac{n^2-1}{12},\quad\operatorname{Var}(cX)=c^2\operatorname{Var}(X)\)
Step 1: \(\sigma^2=4\cdot\dfrac{n^2-1}{12}=\dfrac{n^2-1}{3}\)
Step 2: \(\dfrac{n^2-1}{3}=8\Rightarrow n^2=25\)
Worked derivation: \[n=5\]
Check: \[2,4,6,8,10:\ \bar x=6,\ \sigma^2=\frac{16+4+0+4+16}{5}=8\]
Why: \(\displaystyle\frac1n\sum k^2-\left(\frac{n+1}{2}\right)^2=\frac{(n+1)(2n+1)}{6}-\frac{(n+1)^2}{4}=\frac{n^2-1}{12}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(n=4:\ \sigma^2=5\); (C) \(n=7:\ \sigma^2=16\); (D) \(n=9:\ \sigma^2=\tfrac{80}{3}\).
Key point: \(\operatorname{Var}(aX+b)=a^2\operatorname{Var}(X)\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: Using principal ranges arcsin∈[−π/2,π/2], arccos∈[0,π], arctan∈(−π/2,π/2), evaluate arcsin(sin 7π/6)+arccos(cos 7π/6)+arctan(tan 7π/6).
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 5π/6.
Given: \(\theta=\dfrac{7\pi}{6}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\arcsin\in\left[-\tfrac\pi2,\tfrac\pi2\right],\quad\arccos\in[0,\pi],\quad\arctan\in\left(-\tfrac\pi2,\tfrac\pi2\right)\)
Step 1: \(\sin\dfrac{7\pi}{6}=-\dfrac12\Rightarrow\arcsin\left(-\dfrac12\right)=-\dfrac\pi6\)
Step 2: \(\cos\dfrac{7\pi}{6}=-\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\Rightarrow\arccos\left(-\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)=\dfrac{5\pi}{6}\)
Step 3: \(\tan\dfrac{7\pi}{6}=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt3}\Rightarrow\arctan\dfrac{1}{\sqrt3}=\dfrac\pi6\)
Worked derivation: \[-\frac\pi6+\frac{5\pi}{6}+\frac\pi6=\frac{5\pi}{6}\]
Check: \[\arcsin(\sin\theta)=\pi-\theta,\ \arccos(\cos\theta)=2\pi-\theta,\ \arctan(\tan\theta)=\theta-\pi\ \text{at}\ \theta=\tfrac{7\pi}{6}\]
Why: \(\dfrac{7\pi}{6}\ \text{lies outside all three principal ranges}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\dfrac\pi2\ne\dfrac{5\pi}{6}\); (C) \(\dfrac{7\pi}{6}\notin[0,\pi]\) (\(\arccos(\cos\theta)=\theta\) assumed); (D) \(-\dfrac\pi6+\dfrac{7\pi}{6}+0=\pi\) (same error).
Key point: \(f^{-1}(f(\theta))=\theta\ \text{only on the principal range}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: Blocks of mass 4 kg and 6 kg rest in contact on a smooth horizontal floor. A horizontal force of 20 N pushes on the 4 kg block so that it presses against the 6 kg block. What is the contact force between the blocks?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 12 N.
Given: \(m_1=4\ \mathrm{kg},\quad m_2=6\ \mathrm{kg},\quad F=20\ \mathrm N\ \text{on }m_1,\quad\text{smooth floor}\)
Formula/Principle: \(a=\dfrac{F}{m_1+m_2},\quad N=m_2a\)
Step 1: \(a=\dfrac{20}{4+6}=2\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\)
Step 2: \(m_2:\ N=m_2a\)
Worked derivation: \[N=6\times2=12\ \mathrm N\]
Check: \[m_1:\ F-N=20-12=8\ \mathrm N=4\times2\]
Why: \(\text{the contact force is the only horizontal force on }m_2\)
Why not the others: (A) \(N=F=20\ \mathrm N\) (\(m_1a\) omitted); (B) \(m_1a=8\ \mathrm N\) (net force on \(m_1\)); (D) \(\dfrac F2=10\ \mathrm N\) (equal masses assumed).
Key point: \(N=\dfrac{m_2}{m_1+m_2}F\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: A 1 kg block starts from rest 2 m above a horizontal rough track. After descending a smooth ramp, it travels 3 m across a rough stretch with μ=0.20, then compresses a spring of k=100 N m⁻¹ on the same rough surface. With g=10 m s⁻², which equation and approximate maximum compression x are correct?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 50x²+2x=14, x≈0.51 m.
Given: \(m=1\ \mathrm{kg},\ h=2\ \mathrm m,\ d=3\ \mathrm m,\ \mu=0.20,\ k=100\ \mathrm{N\,m^{-1}},\ g=10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\)
Formula/Principle: \(mgh-\mu mg(d+x)=\tfrac12kx^2\)
Step 1: \(mgh=1\times10\times2=20\ \mathrm J\)
Step 2: \(\mu mgd=0.20\times10\times3=6\ \mathrm J\)
Step 3: \(\mu mgx=2x,\quad\tfrac12kx^2=50x^2\)
Step 4: \(20-6-2x=50x^2\Rightarrow50x^2+2x=14\)
Worked derivation: \[x=\frac{-2+\sqrt{4+4(50)(14)}}{100}=\frac{-2+52.95}{100}=0.51\ \mathrm m\]
Check: \[50(0.51)^2+2(0.51)=13.0+1.02=14.0\ \mathrm J\]
Why: \(\text{friction also acts over the compression distance }x\)
Why not the others: (A) \(50x^2=20\) (all friction omitted); (B) \(50x^2=14\) (friction over \(x\) omitted); (C) \(6x\ne\mu mgx=2x\).
Key point: \(W_{\text{friction}}=-\mu mg\times(\text{total rough distance})\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: Inside a uniform-density planet of radius R, gravitational acceleration at distance R/3 from the centre is what fraction of surface g?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 1/3.
Given: \(\text{uniform density }\rho,\ \text{radius }R,\ r=\dfrac R3\)
Formula/Principle: \(g(r)=\dfrac{GM(r)}{r^2},\quad M(r)=\tfrac43\pi r^3\rho\)
Step 1: \(g(r)=\tfrac43\pi G\rho\,r\)
Step 2: \(g(R)=\tfrac43\pi G\rho\,R\)
Worked derivation: \[\frac{g(R/3)}{g(R)}=\frac{R/3}{R}=\frac13\]
Check: \[r\to0:\ g\to0\]
Why: \(\text{the shell outside radius }r\ \text{exerts no net force}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\left(\tfrac13\right)^2=\tfrac19\) (\(g\propto r^2\)); (C) \(1\) (\(g\) constant); (D) \(3\) (\(g\propto\tfrac1r\)).
Key point: \(\text{inside a uniform sphere }g\propto r\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: Read the two-regime stress–strain plot. Which elastic modulus follows from the initial straight segment?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 50 GPa.
Given: \(\text{from the figure: end of the straight segment at }(\varepsilon,\sigma)=(0.002,\ 100\ \mathrm{MPa})\)
Formula/Principle: \(Y=\dfrac{\sigma}{\varepsilon}\ \ (\text{slope of the linear segment})\)
Step 1: \(Y=\dfrac{100\times10^{6}\ \mathrm{Pa}}{0.002}\)
Worked derivation: \[Y=5.0\times10^{10}\ \mathrm{Pa}=50\ \mathrm{GPa}\]
Check: \[\varepsilon=0.001:\ \sigma=Y\varepsilon=50\ \mathrm{MPa}\ \ (\text{midpoint of the segment})\]
Why: \(\text{Hooke's law holds only on the initial straight segment}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(20\ \mathrm{GPa}=\dfrac{100\ \mathrm{MPa}}{0.005}\); (C) \(100\ \mathrm{GPa}=\dfrac{100\ \mathrm{MPa}}{0.001}\); (D) \(200\ \mathrm{GPa}=\dfrac{100\ \mathrm{MPa}}{0.0005}\).
Key point: \(Y=\text{slope of stress against strain in the elastic region}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: A 100 g ice sample at 0°C is mixed in an insulated vessel with 100 g water at 50°C. Take water c=4.2 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹ and ice latent heat L=334 J g⁻¹. What is the final state?
options: A) All ice melts and water reaches 5°C
C) About 63 g ice melts; mixture remains at 0°C
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) About 63 g ice melts; mixture remains at 0°C.
Given: \(m_i=100\ \mathrm g\ (0^\circ\mathrm C),\ m_w=100\ \mathrm g\ (50^\circ\mathrm C),\ c=4.2\ \mathrm{J\,g^{-1}K^{-1}},\ L=334\ \mathrm{J\,g^{-1}}\)
Formula/Principle: \(Q_{\text{available}}=m_wc\,\Delta T,\quad Q_{\text{melt all}}=m_iL\)
Step 1: \(Q_{\text{available}}=100\times4.2\times50=21\,000\ \mathrm J\)
Step 2: \(Q_{\text{melt all}}=100\times334=33\,400\ \mathrm J>21\,000\ \mathrm J\)
Step 3: \(\text{ice remains}\Rightarrow T_f=0^\circ\mathrm C\)
Worked derivation: \[m_{\text{melted}}=\frac{21\,000}{334}=62.9\ \mathrm g\approx63\ \mathrm g\]
Check: \[62.9\times334=21\,000\ \mathrm J\]
Why: \(Q_{\text{available}}<Q_{\text{melt all}}\Rightarrow\text{ice and water coexist at }0^\circ\mathrm C\)
Why not the others: (A) \(T_f=5^\circ\mathrm C\ \text{needs}\ 33\,400+100(4.2)(5)=35\,500\ \mathrm J>21\,000\ \mathrm J\); (B) \(33\,400\ \mathrm J>21\,000\ \mathrm J\); (D) \(21\,000\ \mathrm J>0\).
Key point: \(\text{compare the heat available with the heat needed to melt all the ice}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: An ideal-gas mixture contains equal numbers of molecules of gases X and Y at a common temperature; their molar masses are 4 and 16 units. If vY is the rms speed of species Y, what is the rms speed computed over all molecules in the mixture divided by vY?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) √(5/2).
Given: \(N_X=N_Y,\quad M_X=4,\quad M_Y=16,\quad\text{same }T\)
Formula/Principle: \(\langle v^2\rangle_i=\dfrac{3RT}{M_i},\quad\langle v^2\rangle_{\text{mix}}=\dfrac{N_X\langle v^2\rangle_X+N_Y\langle v^2\rangle_Y}{N_X+N_Y}\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{\langle v^2\rangle_X}{\langle v^2\rangle_Y}=\dfrac{M_Y}{M_X}=4\)
Step 2: \(\langle v^2\rangle_{\text{mix}}=\dfrac{4v_Y^2+v_Y^2}{2}=\dfrac52v_Y^2\)
Worked derivation: \[\frac{v_{\text{rms,mix}}}{v_Y}=\sqrt{\frac52}\approx1.58\]
Check: \[v_Y<v_{\text{rms,mix}}<v_X=2v_Y\]
Why: \(\text{rms}:\ \text{average the squares, then take the root}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\tfrac12=\dfrac{v_Y}{v_X}\); (B) \(1\) (\(v_{\text{mix}}=v_Y\)); (C) \(\sqrt2\).
Key point: \(v_{\text{rms}}=\sqrt{\langle v^2\rangle}\ne\langle v_{\text{rms}}\rangle\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Infer lift acceleration from period before calculating support force
questions.question: Pendulum P has length L in a stationary laboratory. Pendulum Q has length L/2 in a lift accelerating vertically upward at unknown a. Their measured small-oscillation periods satisfy \(T_Q/T_P=1/2\). What are a/g and the apparent weight of a stationary mass m on a scale in the lift?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 1; 2mg.
Given: \(P:\ L,\ g;\quad Q:\ \dfrac L2,\ g_{\text{eff}}=g+a;\quad\dfrac{T_Q}{T_P}=\dfrac12\)
Formula/Principle: \(T=2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{L}{g_{\text{eff}}}},\quad N=m(g+a)\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{T_Q}{T_P}=\sqrt{\dfrac{L/2}{g+a}\cdot\dfrac gL}=\sqrt{\dfrac{g}{2(g+a)}}\)
Step 2: \(\dfrac{g}{2(g+a)}=\dfrac14\Rightarrow g+a=2g\)
Worked derivation: \[\frac ag=1;\qquad N=m(g+a)=2mg\]
Check: \[T_Q=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{L/2}{2g}}=\frac12\cdot2\pi\sqrt{\frac Lg}\]
Why: \(\text{in a lift accelerating upward},\ g_{\text{eff}}=g+a\)
Why not the others: (B) \(a=\tfrac g2:\ \dfrac{T_Q}{T_P}=\sqrt{\tfrac13}\); (C) \(a=0:\ \dfrac{T_Q}{T_P}=\sqrt{\tfrac12}\); (D) \(a=3g:\ \dfrac{T_Q}{T_P}=\sqrt{\tfrac18}\).
Key point: \(T\propto\sqrt{\dfrac{L}{g+a}}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: Capacitors C and 2C are in series across an ideal battery V. While the battery remains connected, dielectric of κ=2 completely fills the C capacitor. What is the ratio of the new series charge to the original series charge?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 3/2.
Given: \(C_1=C,\ C_2=2C\ \text{in series across }V;\quad C_1\to\kappa C=2C\)
Formula/Principle: \(C_{\text{eq}}=\dfrac{C_1C_2}{C_1+C_2},\quad Q=C_{\text{eq}}V\)
Step 1: \(C_{\text{eq},i}=\dfrac{C\cdot2C}{3C}=\dfrac{2C}{3}\)
Step 2: \(C_{\text{eq},f}=\dfrac{2C\cdot2C}{4C}=C\)
Worked derivation: \[\frac{Q_f}{Q_i}=\frac{CV}{\tfrac23CV}=\frac32\]
Check: \[V_1+V_2=\frac{CV}{2C}+\frac{CV}{2C}=V\]
Why: \(\text{battery connected}\Rightarrow V\ \text{fixed},\ Q\ \text{changes}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(1\) (\(Q\) fixed: isolated case); (C) \(\tfrac23\) (inverted); (D) \(2\) (\(Q\propto C_1\) only).
Key point: \(\text{series capacitors carry equal charge }Q=C_{\text{eq}}V\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Moving Charges and Magnetism / Magnetism and Matter
questions.sub_topic: Radius and period of a charged particle in a magnetic field
questions.question: A proton moves in a circle in a uniform magnetic field. Its speed is doubled, with the field unchanged. What happens to the radius of the circle and to the period of revolution?
options: B) The radius is unchanged; the period halves
C) The radius doubles; the period is unchanged
D) The radius halves; the period doubles
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) The radius doubles; the period is unchanged.
Given: \(v\to2v,\quad B,\ q,\ m\ \text{unchanged},\quad\mathbf v\perp\mathbf B\)
Formula/Principle: \(qvB=\dfrac{mv^2}{r}\Rightarrow r=\dfrac{mv}{qB},\quad T=\dfrac{2\pi r}{v}=\dfrac{2\pi m}{qB}\)
Step 1: \(r'=\dfrac{m(2v)}{qB}=2r\)
Worked derivation: \[T'=\frac{2\pi(2r)}{2v}=\frac{2\pi m}{qB}=T\]
Check: \[\text{proton},\ B=1\ \mathrm T:\ T=\frac{2\pi(1.67\times10^{-27})}{(1.6\times10^{-19})(1)}=6.6\times10^{-8}\ \mathrm s\ \ (\text{no }v)\]
Why: \(\text{circumference}\propto v\Rightarrow T\ \text{independent of }v\)
Why not the others: (A) \(T'=T\ne2T\); (B) \(r'=2r\ne r\); (D) \(r\propto v,\ \text{not}\ \tfrac1v\).
Key point: \(r=\dfrac{mv}{qB},\quad T=\dfrac{2\pi m}{qB}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Electric Charges and Fields / Electrostatic Potential
questions.question: A permanent electric dipole p in uniform E is initially perpendicular to the field and rotates into alignment without friction. How do its torque magnitude and potential energy change between these endpoints?
options: B) Torque stays maximum; energy decreases
C) Torque falls to zero; energy increases
D) Torque falls to zero; energy decreases
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Torque falls to zero; energy decreases.
Given: \(\theta_i=90^\circ,\quad\theta_f=0^\circ\)
Formula/Principle: \(\tau=pE\sin\theta,\quad U=-pE\cos\theta\)
Step 1: \(\tau_i=pE\sin90^\circ=pE,\quad\tau_f=pE\sin0^\circ=0\)
Step 2: \(U_i=-pE\cos90^\circ=0,\quad U_f=-pE\cos0^\circ=-pE\)
Worked derivation: \[\Delta\tau=-pE;\qquad\Delta U=-pE-0=-pE<0\]
Check: \[\Delta K=-\Delta U=+pE>0\]
Why: \(\theta=0\ \text{is the stable equilibrium}:\ \tau=0,\ U=U_{\min}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\tau_f=0<\tau_i\); (B) \(\tau_f=0\ne pE\); (C) \(\Delta U=-pE<0\).
Key point: \(\tau=\mathbf p\times\mathbf E,\quad U=-\mathbf p\cdot\mathbf E\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: A Wheatstone bridge has left arms 10 Ω and 15 Ω and right upper arm 20 Ω; the right lower arm is a resistor of 25 Ω at 0°C with temperature coefficient 0.004 °C⁻¹. At what temperature is the bridge balanced?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 50°C.
Given: \(P=10\ \Omega,\ Q=15\ \Omega\ (\text{left});\quad R=20\ \Omega,\ S_0=25\ \Omega\ \text{at }0^\circ\mathrm C,\ \alpha=0.004\ ^\circ\mathrm C^{-1}\ (\text{right})\)
Formula/Principle: \(\dfrac PQ=\dfrac RS,\quad S=S_0(1+\alpha T)\)
Step 1: \(S=\dfrac{QR}{P}=\dfrac{15\times20}{10}=30\ \Omega\)
Step 2: \(25(1+0.004T)=30\Rightarrow0.004T=0.20\)
Worked derivation: \[T=\frac{0.20}{0.004}=50\ ^\circ\mathrm C\]
Check: \[\frac{10}{15}=\frac{20}{30}=\frac23\]
Why: \(\text{balance}\iff\text{no potential difference across the galvanometer}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(25^\circ\mathrm C:\ S=27.5\ \Omega\); (C) \(75^\circ\mathrm C:\ S=32.5\ \Omega\); (D) \(100^\circ\mathrm C:\ S=35\ \Omega\).
Key point: \(R_T=R_0(1+\alpha T)\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: Using the indices and incoming angle in the parallel-layer diagram, what happens to the ray at the final layer–air interface?
options: A) Total internal reflection before reaching B
B) It emerges grazing the air surface
C) It emerges into air at 30°
D) It refracts into air at 45°
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) It emerges grazing the air surface.
Given: \(\text{from the figure}:\ n_A=2,\ n_B=\sqrt2,\ n_{\text{air}}=1,\ \theta_A=30^\circ\)
Formula/Principle: \(n\sin\theta=\text{constant across parallel layers}\)
Step 1: \(n_A\sin\theta_A=2\sin30^\circ=1\)
Step 2: \(\sqrt2\sin\theta_B=1\Rightarrow\theta_B=45^\circ\)
Step 3: \(1\cdot\sin\theta_{\text{air}}=1\)
Worked derivation: \[\theta_{\text{air}}=90^\circ\ \ (\text{grazing emergence})\]
Check: \[\theta_c(B\to\text{air})=\sin^{-1}\frac{1}{\sqrt2}=45^\circ=\theta_B\]
Why: \(\text{incidence exactly at the critical angle}\Rightarrow\text{refracted ray along the surface}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\theta_c(A\to B)=\sin^{-1}\dfrac{\sqrt2}{2}=45^\circ>30^\circ\Rightarrow\text{transmitted into }B\); (C) \(\sin30^\circ=\tfrac12\ne1\); (D) \(\sin45^\circ=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\ne1\).
Key point: \(n_1\sin\theta_1=n_2\sin\theta_2=n_3\sin\theta_3\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: From the stopping-potential plot for a metal, infer its work function in electronvolts.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 2 eV.
Given: \(\text{from the figure}:\ V_s=0\ \text{at}\ f_0=5\times10^{14}\ \mathrm{Hz};\quad V_s=1\ \mathrm V\ \text{at}\ f=7.5\times10^{14}\ \mathrm{Hz}\)
Formula/Principle: \(eV_s=hf-\phi\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac he=\dfrac{\Delta V_s}{\Delta f}=\dfrac{1}{2.5\times10^{14}}=4\times10^{-15}\ \mathrm{V\,s}\)
Step 2: \(\phi=hf_0\)
Worked derivation: \[\frac{\phi}{e}=\frac he f_0=4\times10^{-15}\times5\times10^{14}=2\ \mathrm V\Rightarrow\phi=2\ \mathrm{eV}\]
Check: \[f=7.5\times10^{14}:\ hf=3\ \mathrm{eV},\ eV_s=3-2=1\ \mathrm{eV}\]
Why: \(\text{the intercept on the frequency axis is the threshold frequency}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(0.5\ \mathrm{eV}\ne hf_0\); (B) \(1\ \mathrm{eV}=eV_s\ \text{at}\ 7.5\times10^{14}\ \mathrm{Hz}\); (D) \(4\ \mathrm{eV}=2hf_0\).
Key point: \(\text{slope}=\dfrac he,\quad\text{x-intercept}=f_0=\dfrac\phi h\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Path mixture inferred from photon count and mean photon energy
questions.question: One hundred atoms start at hydrogen level n=4. Each reaches n=2 either by direct 4→2 emission A or by the two-step cascade 4→3→2 shown. Exactly 150 photons are emitted in total. Neglect all other paths. What fraction of atoms took the direct path, and what is the mean emitted-photon energy divided by the energy of photon A?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 1/2; 2/3.
Given: \(100\ \text{atoms at }n=4;\quad\text{direct }4\to2\ (1\ \text{photon});\quad4\to3\to2\ (2\ \text{photons});\quad150\ \text{photons}\)
Formula/Principle: \(E_{4\to2}=E_{4\to3}+E_{3\to2}=E_A\)
Step 1: \(x+2(100-x)=150\Rightarrow x=50\)
Step 2: \(\text{fraction direct}=\dfrac{50}{100}=\dfrac12\)
Step 3: \(E_{\text{total}}=100E_A\ \ (\text{each atom releases }E_A)\)
Worked derivation: \[\frac{\langle E\rangle}{E_A}=\frac{100E_A}{150E_A}=\frac23\]
Check: \[E_A=13.6\left(\tfrac14-\tfrac1{16}\right)=2.55\ \mathrm{eV};\quad0.66+1.89=2.55\ \mathrm{eV}\]
Why: \(\text{energy released depends only on the initial and final levels}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\langle E\rangle=E_A\ \text{needs 100 photons}\); (B) \(x=25:\ 25+150=175\ne150\); (C) \(\dfrac{150}{100}=\dfrac32\) (inverted).
Key point: \(\langle E\rangle=\dfrac{\text{total energy}}{\text{number of photons}}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Charge that flows when the flux through a coil changes
questions.question: A coil of 100 turns and resistance 10 Ω forms a closed circuit. The magnetic flux through each turn changes from 0.02 Wb to 0.05 Wb in 0.10 s. How much charge flows through the coil?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 0.30 C.
Given: \(N=100,\quad R=10\ \Omega,\quad\Phi_i=0.02\ \mathrm{Wb},\quad\Phi_f=0.05\ \mathrm{Wb},\quad\Delta t=0.10\ \mathrm s\)
Formula/Principle: \(\varepsilon=N\dfrac{\Delta\Phi}{\Delta t},\quad I=\dfrac\varepsilon R,\quad q=I\,\Delta t=\dfrac{N\,\Delta\Phi}{R}\)
Step 1: \(\varepsilon=100\times\dfrac{0.03}{0.10}=30\ \mathrm V\)
Step 2: \(I=\dfrac{30}{10}=3.0\ \mathrm A\)
Worked derivation: \[q=3.0\times0.10=0.30\ \mathrm C\]
Check: \[q=\frac{N\,\Delta\Phi}{R}=\frac{100\times0.03}{10}=0.30\ \mathrm C\ \ (\text{no }\Delta t)\]
Why: \(q=\displaystyle\int I\,dt=\frac NR\int\frac{d\Phi}{dt}\,dt\)
Why not the others: (B) \(3.0=I\ \text{in A}\); (C) \(\dfrac{\Delta\Phi}{R}=0.003\ \mathrm C\) (\(N\) omitted); (D) \(30=\varepsilon\ \text{in V}\).
Key point: \(q=\dfrac{N\,\Delta\Phi}{R}\)
